stories.title: Mental health order for teen charged over Tyrone murder
stories.summary: A judge has ordered a mental health assessment of a teenage boy charged with the murder of a 61-year-old man and the attempted murder of the man's wife and daughter in Co Tyrone. The man was killed and his eight-year-old daughter severely injured in an attack in their home in Lisnahull Road in Dungannon on Saturday morning. She is now in a stable condition in hospital. The girl's mother also sustained non-life-threatening injuries. The 16-year-old boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, appeared in a youth court in Omagh for a short hearing this morning. He is charged with murder, two attempted murders and threats to kill. The teenager spoke only to confirm that he understood the charges.

stories.title: Man, 21, jailed over 'brutal' murder of Cork postman
stories.summary: A 21-year-old man has been sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Cork postman Barry Daly, in what was described by the judge as a "brutal action". Alex Deady of Glen View, Convent Road in Doneraile, was last month convicted of murdering Mr Daly, a father-of-five, in the early hours of Sunday 12 October last year, outside his home at Rockview Terrace in Doneraile. Mr Daly, who was 44, died of catastrophic head and facial injuries that were inflicted with a golf club. Deady and two teenage boys, who cannot be named because of their age, went on trial in June charged with the murder. Deady and the older teenager, who is 17, pleaded guilty to the manslaughter of Mr Daly but not guilty to his murder. During the trial the other teenager, who is 16, entered a plea of not guilty to murder but guilty to manslaughter. This plea was subsequently accepted by the Director of Public Prosecutions.

stories.title: State-backed investment account offers tax-free threshold
stories.summary: No deemed disposal, a tax-free threshold, and no minimum contribution will be among the key features of the Government's new personal-investment account scheme. It is also understood savers will be able to invest in shares, bonds, and ETFs - however - investing in risky products such as crypto assets and derivatives will not be allowed. Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris is due to announce a roadmap for the new State-backed accounts tomorrow, which are expected to be up and running early next year. Under deemed disposal, every eight years certain investments are treated as if they have been sold for tax purposes - even if there has been no sale. As a result, any gains on such investments are taxed at 38%. The controversial tax is designed to combat tax avoidance. Instead, under the Government's plan, providers will be responsible for calculating, reporting, and paying any tax due to revenue on behalf of investors.

stories.title: Euro zone inflation rises above 3% on higher energy costs
stories.summary: Euro zone inflation rose back above 3% in August on higher energy costs, cementing an already solid case for ⁠another European Central Bank interest rate hike this month as the Iran war keeps putting upward pressure on prices. Inflation in the 21 nations sharing the euro accelerated to 3.3% in August from 2.9% in July, driven almost entirely by higher energy costs as crude oil and natural gas prices both rose, and refiners bumped up their margins, data from Eurostat showed today. Underlying price pressures remained modest, however, offering some reassurance to policymakers that the energy price surge is not yet setting off the kind of second-round effects that could perpetuate rapid inflation and force the ECB into more aggressive action. Indeed, core inflation - figures which exclude volatile food and fuel prices - eased to 2.4% last month from 2.5% as growth in services prices, ‌the single biggest component of the consumer price ⁠basket, slowed to 3% from 3.3%. Today's figures are broadly consistent with the ECB's own expectations and suggest that a widely telegraphed hike in the deposit rate to 2.50% on September 10, the bank's second move this year after a hike in June, will be a relatively easy decision, almost a non-event for markets. Financial investors have already priced in the move, suggesting that their focus will be on the rate path further down the line, a ‌more complicated issue as views diverge on just how deep the euro zone's inflation problems run.

stories.title: Trump threatens to hit Iran 'hard' as hostilities resume
stories.summary: Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "hard" after the two foes traded fire for the first time in over a month, while Iran's president warned that more fighting with the US was not in his country's interest. After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and the US persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran. Last night, the United States said it had carried out strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran said had killed two people and, with Tehran quickly retaliating by attacking US military targets in the Middle East. The exchange raised fears of a return to major hostilities, with the US president vowing to respond. "We're going to hit them hard," Mr Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. "There will be a response." The United States said it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the key shipping lane. Iranian state media said the attack had killed two people and wounded several others.

stories.title: Ballygunner survive Fourmilewater scare to retain title
stories.summary: Ballygunner are kings of Waterford hurling for the 13th year running, but it was very much an unlucky 13 as they had to overcome a ferocious effort from rivals Fourmilewater to win out by four points at the finish. Trailing by three points with 53 minutes on the clock, the All-Ireland champions drew from every inch of their experience to outscore the Nire men 1-4 to nil down the home straight to march on to Munster once again - Mark Hartley's added-time goal ensuring another piece of silverware for Jason Ryan’s side. Playing in a 14th consecutive county decider, the Gunners arrived seeking a 13th News & Star Cup on the spin - facing a seventh different final opponent in the form of Fourmilewater, who themselves reached the last hurdle for the very first time in their 100-year history. Fourmilewater started the brighter, Sean Walsh getting out first to a breaking ball to split the posts with a minute played, but a great catch and score from Dessie Hutchinson soon drew the Gunners level. A superb effort on the left flank from Michael Morrissey was cancelled out by Conor Tobin, but Fourmilewater clicked into gear from here in what was a somewhat attritional beginning - bringing extreme physicality exemplified by Conor Gleeson, Dermot Ryan and Tholom Guiry. Liam O’Brien swivelled to restore the lead, before Jamie Barron got inside Philip Mahony and Paddy Leavey but his goal-bound strike could only find the side netting. Barron emerged from a ruck to split the posts, before Pauric Mahony opened his account at the other end - and Stephen Ryan had to be on hand to deny Kevin Mahony when sent racing through by Hutchinson.

stories.title: Fernandes hat-trick helps United to thumping Ipswich win
stories.summary: Bruno Fernandes' hat-trick helped Manchester United bounce back from their Hull humiliation and a poor start against Ipswich to secure a 5-2 comeback victory on Sunday. Michael Carrick’s Red Devils suffered a deserved defeat in their Premier League opener last weekend and were facing further embarrassment against promoted opposition at Old Trafford. Leif Davis fired Ipswich ahead but United showed the spirit and intensity sorely lacking at Hull, with Fernandes levelling and Harry Maguire surviving a VAR check for handball after his effort went in off Jacob Greaves. The Ipswich defender soon gave away a penalty that Fernandes converted, before the freshly-crowned PFA Player of the Year completed his hat-trick from close range. Bryan Mbeumo added gloss and Chuba Akpom scored a late consolation for Ipswich on a day when Marcus Rashford made an impressive first Old Trafford appearance in 90 weeks. United paraded new £70 million signing Carlos Baleba, out with an ankle issue, before a match they began brightly as Matheus Cunha lifted over following some enterprising work by Rashford.

stories.title: Buttimer strikes again as Munster retain Interpro title
stories.summary: Beth Buttimer haunted Leinster once again as Munster held off their rivals to retain their Vodafone Women's Interprovincial Championship at Dexcom Stadium. Three weeks on from scoring four tries in her side’s 39-19 win against the same opposition, Buttimer scored two more in today’s final in Galway to make it back-to-back Interpro championships for Matt Brown’s side. The hooker’s first score on 20 minutes had given her side a slender 7-5 lead at half time, with Kathy Baker crossing for Leinster shortly before the break. And it would take until the 70-minute mark for either team to add to their total, as Buttimer touched down from the back of a rolling maul, before Enya Breen landed a high-pressure conversion which put her side nine points ahead, and crucially give them a two-score buffer heading into the closing minutes. The afternoon may well have come at some cost for Ireland head coach Scott Bemand, who saw second row Ruth Campbell limp out of the Leinster side in the opening half. Three weeks out from his team’s opening WXV Global Series game against USA in Tallaght, the Ireland head coach will also have some important decisions to make.

stories.title: Ruth Negga, Ariana Grande and the risk of star-studded theatre
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. It's arguably one of the biggest thrills you can experience in culture: getting to see your screen idol up close, in the flesh and doing what they do best just a few metres away from you. Many Hollywood stars have dipped in and out of theatre over the course of their careers, many returning to tread the boards perhaps in a bid to reconnect with their love of acting or to challenge themselves in front of a living, breathing, reactive audience. And in recent years, it seems that there has arguably been more recognisable names in theatre roles than ever before - whether it’s Paul Mescal in A Streetcar Named Desire (he’ll also return to the National Theatre in London and Dublin’s Abbey Theatre for Tom Murphy’s A Whistle in the Dark in 2027), or George Clooney in Good Night and Good Luck, Keanu Reeves in Waiting for Godot and Denzel Washington & Jake Gyllenhaal in Othello on Broadway. In recent months on Irish shores alone, we’ve seen Matthew Broderick in Ulster American at the Abbey and Chris O’Dowd in The Brightening Air at The Gate, while Brendan Gleeson performed in The Weir at the Olympia Theatre just last year. Perhaps the fallout from Covid has something to do with the increasing trend of theatres landing big names to sell tickets (at increasingly high costs, it must be pointed out); those long months of closures may take years to recover financially from. Another big name that was soon due to take to an Irish stage was Ruth Negga. The Limerick actress was set to lead the cast in Radio Bette, a brand new experimental work by New York-based theatre company The Goat Exchange, which runs at the Gaiety Theatre next month as part of the Dublin Theatre Festival programme. An announcement from The Goat Exchange revealed Negga’s withdrawal from the production, with no specific reason offered. "The Goat Exchange regrets to announce that Ruth Negga will be stepping back from Radio Bette," it read. "We are deeply grateful to Ruth for the time, generosity, and extraordinary work she has brought to the project." Negga herself has not commented on the development. Hopefully all is okay with the actress first and foremost, particularly as it’s not as though she has a habit of being unreliable and presumably there was a genuine reason for her sudden departure. But it does leave the company in something of a quandary and perhaps highlights the risk of casting Big Stars: when you sell tickets to a show - particularly a new and untested one like Radio Bette - off the back of a well-known actress’s name/talent, plugging that gap and keeping audiences happy poses a more significant dilemma than simply ushering in an understudy. Ruth Negga can rest assured, nevertheless, that she is not the first actor to pull out of a show in dramatic fashion, nor will she be the last. Only last month, Ariana Grande withdrew from the Barbican’s production of Stephen Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George, in which she was due to make her West End debut opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in 2027. Grande cited a desire to take "a step back from visibility" following the conclusion of her current tour; a "much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny", according to her publicist. Who’d be famous, eh?

stories.title: Oran Aurelio on designing CMAT's Electric Picnic outfit
stories.summary: Charlotte Ryan speaks to Irish designer Oran Aurelio about creating CMAT's Electric Picnic outfit, evolving his iconic looks for The Traitors Ireland and how Irish designers are having their moment. Oran Aurelio is "still on the most insane high ever" after a momentous weekend in his career: designing CMAT's jaw-dropping stage outfit for her electrifying Electric Picnic appearance, and seeing his reworked designs on the premiere of season two of The Traitors Ireland. Although his client list includes Chappell Roan, Addison Rae and Ariana Madix, it's clear that his Irish collaborators are especially dear to Aurelio's heart. Last weekend's Electric Picnic was a particularly notable moment for the Dublin-based designer. A year to the day after the release of her celebrated album Euro-Country, CMAT - whose real name is Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson - stepped out on stage in an eye-catching vivid blue leotard and detachable skirt that paid homage to the blue velvet gown Aurelio designed for the album cover. Recalling getting the invite to collaborate on the star's stage look, Aurelio says it was "the most no-brainer decision I've ever had to make".

stories.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet flash floods passes 1,000
stories.summary: Devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 987 people in Nepal, the country's disaster authority has said, taking the number of overall deaths to more than 1,000. Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 people were killed in Tibet, bringing the total toll from last week's disaster to 1,003. The number of people missing in Nepal dropped to 3,916, as rescue efforts entered a seventh day, and the bodies recovered rose. In China, state media say there 546 people missing, taking the number of missing to 4,462. The missing in Nepal include 583 foreign nationals from over 30 nationalities. Two Irish citizens, who have been named by the Nepalese Tourism Department as 46-year-old Santosh Sahu and 18-year-old Spandan Sahu, are among those missing. The missing in China includes 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries.

stories.title: Tánaiste to meet G20 finance ministers in US
stories.summary: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris will meet G20 finance ministers in the US as part of Ireland's ongoing EU presidency role. The two-day trip in North Carolina will include meetings with Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey and Canada's Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne. The event sees finance ministers and Central Bank governors from the G20 nations meet to discuss the global economy, with additional interest this week on individual countries' energy security and financial stability. As part of Ireland's EU presidency role, Mr Harris is attending alongside European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde and EU Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis. Meanwhile, further EU presidency meetings will take place in Ireland this week involving defence and foreign ministers from EU member states. This evening, defence ministers from 17 EU member states will arrive in Ireland for an informal summit chaired by Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence Helen McEntee.

stories.title: State lacks dedicated strategy for children in care
stories.summary: As Autumn approaches and the news cycle moves on, questions over the M9 crash will likely fade. Not so for the injured family and their loved ones, the tragedy of that Sunday morning is something they will have to endure for a lifetime. Five families who lost teenagers in the crash, including three members of the Traveller Community, will continue to process their loss. This week, Tánaiste Simon Harris described the issues raised by the crash as "deep-rooted" and "multifaceted", extending across social media, Government, the criminal justice system and road safety. No mention of the care system which formed part of three of the boys' lives; or the juvenile detention centre, Oberstown, which was familiar to one of the teenagers. On the same day he made his remarks, 17-year-old Jack Kennedy’s funeral was under way in Athy. It was the final funeral of the five.

stories.title: Factory activity robust in August as new business surges
stories.summary: The manufacturing sector expanded robustly again in August and at close to a four-year high as new orders rose at the sharpest pace since April 2022, the latest AIB Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index shows. The AIB Manufacturing PMI, compiled by S&P Global, rose to 55.4 in August from 55.1 in July. The 50 mark separates growth from contraction. Manufacturing activity has not contracted since December 2024, and growth has accelerated over the past five months at the fastest rate since that run began. While new orders hit a four and a half year high, new business from abroad increased at a much weaker pace for the second successive month due to uncertainty caused by the war in the Middle East. The conflict also contributed to continued supply-chain delays, with the sharp rate of deterioration in suppliers' delivery times only slightly softer than in July. Meanwhile, delays receiving purchased items caused a further build-up in backlogs of work, the fifth in the past six months.

stories.title: Nepal flood toll tops 900 as number of missing climbs
stories.summary: The death toll following devastating floods in Nepal has surpassed 900, as rescue teams worked overnight to reach hundreds of people believed to be stuck inside blocked hydropower project tunnels. The devastating floods near the border with China have killed at least 939 people in Nepal, while the number of missing in the country dropped to 3,925, its disaster authority said, six days after the disaster. Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead and 546 people missing in Tibet, taking the overall toll to 955 dead and 4,471 missing. The unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on the Nepal-Tibet border happened last Wednesday and has been blamed on a glacier collapse. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves as they began decomposing in the humid weather in the plains of the Himalayan country after being swept down the mountains by the torrent. Nepal's disaster agency listed 3,333 missing citizens in its update.

stories.title: Team Ireland Euro squad taking inspiration from Taylor
stories.summary: It's the hottest ticket in town, but for the cream of Irish amateur boxing Katie Taylor’s Croke Park extravaganza on Saturday is an event they'll let pass. Monkstown’s Marley has already decided to watch Taylor’s bout from afar with sparring sessions booked in for Friday and Sunday. DCU’s Lehane has a ticket but is leaning that way too. It’s not that Taylor’s fight isn’t important enough to attend. Quite the opposite, the Bray warrior has taken Irish boxing to a new level, and standards have now been set. The potential misuse of a rest day is pretty non-negotiable ahead of competition in Sofia. Whether some of the 14-strong squad make it to Jones’ Road or not, it’s quite clear the impact Taylor has had on the group. Lehane hasn’t met Taylor - a day’s teaching robbing her of the opportunity when the star visited the high performance unit – but she’s been long blown away by her success in the amateur game followed by her incredible transition and progression to the very top of the professional arena. The fact that Taylor has reached such a high level in a number of sports – earning 11 caps for the Republic of Ireland and being a keen ladies footballer and camog – also resonates strongly with Lehane, a multi-European medal winner in taekwondo.

stories.title: Fourmilewater chasing glory to add to the history book
stories.summary: Championship final day is not a rare thing in Ballymacarbry, it's the norm really. When Comeragh Rangers won the 2024 Waterford Ladies SFC final, it ended the greatest winning run in Gaelic Games history with Ballymacarbry winning 42 titles in a row before that. The Nire too have brought senior football titles back to the village, 11 in all since 1993 with eight final losses bringing the appearance record to over 20 in that spell. But hurling? Hurling has had to play second fiddle to who have given their life to the Nire-Fourmilewater GAA and Ballymacarbry LGFA club on the Waterford-Tipperary border. Until now that is, because in its centenary year, Fourmile have reached the Waterford SHC final for the first time in their history with Ballygunner, the heaviest of heavyweights, awaiting in Dungarvan this afternoon. If you want evidence to back that claim up then look no further than the draw for the championship with Ballygunner having an A and B team in the senior pots. The B team, as it happens, managed 3-11 against Fourmilewater in the group stage but were still well short at the final whistle.

stories.title: Hoops come from behind to salvage point in Derry
stories.summary: Two goals in eight second half minutes saw Shamrock Rovers come back from the dead to take a point at the Brandywell. Just days after exiting Europe, Rovers showed their fighting spirit yet again, with Stephen Bradley's second half substitutions - particularly William Fitzgerald and Dylan Watts - proving that they remain the standard in the league. It was at least a better showing from Mark Connolly's players than last week’s second half collapse against Bohemians, but City have now wasted half-time leads in their last two games, taking just one point in the process. The most notable chance from the City team which lost to Bohemians last week was in goal, as Reading loanee Tom Norcott came in for his debut in place of Brian Maher, who was only fit enough to make the substitutes’ bench. Derry City wasted no time in opening the scoring when Ellis Chapman won the ball from Lee Grace and immediately fed Michael Duffy, who raced into the area from the left and pulled it back for Chapman to sweep in his fourth goal for the club. The goal was timed at 81 seconds, City’s quickest goal of the season. The lead was doubled when John O’Sullivan lost possession too easily, eased off the ball 25 yards from goal by Chapman, and Darragh Burns took over, slipping the ball in behind for Duffy, who fired the ball past Ed McGinty for his fourth goal in three games.

stories.title: Star Trek at 60: its secret was exploring humanity, not aliens
stories.summary: When Star Trek first appeared on television screens 60 years ago, audiences expected science fiction to offer aliens, monsters and futuristic technology, writes Stephen McVeigh. From its very first broadcast episode on September 8 1966, Star Trek established that its true subject was the exploration of humanity itself. For all its reputation as an action-packed space adventure, the franchise has endured because it repeatedly returned to a universal question: what does it mean to be human? In that first episode, entitled The Man Trap, the alien antagonist survives by appearing to each observer as the person they most wish to see. Dr Leonard "Bones" McCoy meets a lost love from his past; others see figures shaped by memory, expectation, desire and longing. The creature, soon dubbed the "salt vampire" by fans of the series, is not simply a shape-shifter. Its power lies in exploiting human perception. Rather than asking viewers to fear an alien with superior strength or advanced weaponry, the episode asks a more profound question: can we trust our experience of reality? Watch a clip from The Man Trap, the first Star Trek episode to air in September 1966 Sixty years on, this question looks remarkably prescient. Modern neuroscience increasingly suggests that perception is not a passive recording of the external world. According to theories of predictive processing, the brain continually generates expectations and compares them with incoming sensory information.

stories.title: Lancaster says Rod Stewart will 'come back stronger'
stories.summary: Penny Lancaster has said husband Rod Stewart will "come back stronger than ever" following a heart operation which saw him cancel tour dates. Lancaster said Stewart, 81, "can’t wait to see his fans again" having had "so many wonderful well wishes and support", after he cut short his tour in the US and Mexico this year, which was due to stretch into September. She told the Press Association: "He’s back at full speed in his day-to-day activities, but doctor’s orders were to kind of postpone or cancel the current tour, because you know the risk factors involved. "I did have to explain to the doctor what Rod’s performances are like, he doesn’t just sit down on a stool or behind a piano, he runs around for nearly two hours with four different costume changes because he’s sweating through everything. "So, I compared him to either a boxer coming out of his dressing room on the way to the ring, or either a horse coming out the blocks, I mean, he runs on and he’s like, you know, straight into it, 100 miles an hour and doesn’t stop. "It’s like running a sprint for him, so just for precaution that tour unfortunately had to be cancelled, which he was devastated about.

stories.title: Met Gala exhibit honouring John Galliano cancelled amid backlash
stories.summary: John Galliano has pulled out of the 2027 Met Gala, and the career-spanning exhibition that the high-profile event would kickstart next May, amid mounting backlash over his past racist and antisemitic comments. Organised by Andrew Bolton, Curator in Charge of the Costume Institute in New York City, John Galliano: Horizons was due to open on 3 May and celebrate Galliano's work and influence on the fashion industry across four decades. Galliano would have been only the third living designer to receive the honour, following Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017. However, the controversial designer announced today that he would not take part in the exhibition, sharing in a statement on his Instagram that, "After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time". In an article on Vogue, it was reported that the exhibition "will not proceed as planned", but it is unknown what that currently means for next year's Met Gala. The decision comes after weeks of backlash from members of the Jewish community, who criticised the Met's decision to go ahead with the exhibition in light of Galliano's past comments, for which he was convicted in France.

stories.title: Security tight as EU defence ministers meeting in Wicklow
stories.summary: EU defence ministers have gathered in Co Wicklow for an informal meeting as part of Ireland's hosting of the Presidency of the European Council. There will be an increased garda presence, road closures and airspace restrictions in the area. Minister for Defence Helen McEntee is likely to discuss a range of issues with her European counterparts including EU support for Ukraine, Lebanon and maritime security. The gathering comes after Taoiseach Micheál Martin said last week that one of Ireland's priorities during the EU Presidency was to "unequivocally back Ukraine" as it continues to face attacks from Russia. Ms McEntee will host an informal meeting of ministers from 27 EU member states - chaired by the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas - before hosting a press conference this afternoon. Ministers meeting at the Druids Glen resort will also likely focus on the latest developments in the US war against Iran, after the US this week carried out what it called targeted strikes to tackle an imminent threat from Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.title: Calls for 'full cost review' into Govt's carbon tax plans
stories.summary: Fuels for Ireland has urged the Government not to "weaken" long-stated carbon tax plans without "a full cost review" of the potential measure. In recent days, the group has suggested that the Coalition could slow down the timing of planned carbon tax increases as part of October's budget. Under existing plans linked to climate action initiatives, the Government is due to increase carbon taxes resulting in a €53.50 rise in the price of home heating oil, a €4.86 rise in the price of a tank of petrol and a €5.76 rise in a tank of diesel by the end of the decade. However, with planned increases over summer being postponed due to Middle East war, it has been suggested further increases could also now be delayed. Responding to the rumours, Fuels for Ireland's Chief Executive Kevin McPartlan told the Government: "Carbon tax has a clear emissions-reduction purpose. Before Government changes its trajectory, it should examine the whole fuel-policy system, what each measure costs, what it delivers and how the measures interact. "If Government believes the total burden on motorists, businesses and households has become too high, it seems strange the next measure we might slow down is carbon tax without first examining everything else Government policy adds to the price of fuel.

stories.title: Carbon Tax U-turn, EP on TDs' minds for brief Dáil return
stories.summary: There was such a level of new season energy in the Dáil yesterday that the Ceann Comhairle momentarily forgot to have the customary opening moment of reflection. The half a minute period where deputies gather their thoughts or perhaps ponder on deep existential questions was cast aside. Once the ball was thrown in, the focus turned to one of the most ponderable of subjects, the question of time. The Opposition universally believed there was not enough of it to sign off on that plan to pause excise rates on petrol and diesel until November. The outline schedule for the day had pencilled in a flimsy one hour for this most rare of things, a Dáil sitting in August. Afterall, the return to this place of work usually coincides with the swallows' departure from these shores in the latter part of September.

stories.title: John Ternus to lead Apple into the age of AI
stories.summary: John Ternus takes over as Apple's chief executive today, inheriting a company that towers over the smartphone market but trails its rivals in artificial intelligence. One of his biggest challenges will be balancing the company's dependence on China while parrying acute political pressure from the White House. The handover ends Tim Cook's 15-year run, replacing the operations specialist who built Apple's supply chain with the engineer who built its hardware. Ternus, 51, joined Apple's design team in 2001 and worked his way up to senior vice president of hardware engineering, reporting to Cook. He leads the engineering teams behind Apple's entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company's revenue. He gets barely a week to settle in, with Apple holding its annual iPhone event on September 9, where it is expected to unveil its first foldable handset.

stories.title: Profitable Croke Park Taylor made for entertaining masses
stories.summary: "It's not often I'm lost for words," Eddie Hearn announced at the start of his nine-minute monologue at the Taylor-Pili fight press conference at Croke Park last June. "The last person to fight at this incredible stadium? Mohammad Ali," Hearn said, confirming that the many editions of the international rules series had passed him by. When Ali fought Al 'Blue' Lewis in Croke Park in July 1972, he was treated beforehand like a visiting leader of a foreign superpower. He was mobbed by admirers at Leinster House and had a private meeting with Jack Lynch. He had a lengthy televised sit-down interview with Cathal O'Shannon. Eddie Keher taught him the basics of hurling. Ali himself was very anxious to meet Bernadette Devlin and she had lunch with him on the day of the fight, where they discussed politics, a subject on which they were perfectly aligned. From Hearn's perspective, the bout could have served as a cautionary tale.
